choices.A: He declares that he has judged the noblemen’s conduct in an impartial manner, and that despite their attempts to regain his trust through professions of submissiveness, they have irrevocably lost his respect.
choices.B: He acknowledges to the noblemen that his tolerance of their conduct has undermined their respect for him, and he resolves to display his genuine nature, which is more forceful and compels deference.
choices.C: He defends his calm disposition, which he sees as fundamental to his personality, and vows to maintain his tranquil demeanor even if it causes him to lose the respect of overly proud noblemen.
choices.D: He concedes that he has treated the noblemen with indifference, which in part explains why they have defied him, but he asserts that their disrespectful behavior is primarily driven by their excessive pride.

rationale: Choice B is the best answer because it most accurately describes King Henry’s self-presentation in the text. Henry states that his temperament has been “too cold and temperate, / Unapt to stir at these indignities” (that is, too calm and slow to react to insults), and he asserts that the noblemen have taken advantage of this: “accordingly / You tread upon my patience.” He then resolves to change, declaring he will “from henceforth rather be myself, / Mighty and to be fear’d,” since being lenient (“smooth as oil, soft as young down”) has caused him to lose “that title of respect / Which the proud soul ne’er pays but to the proud.” In other words, Henry recognizes that proud people like the noblemen respect only strength and resolves to show his more forceful, true nature.

Choice A is incorrect because the text doesn’t describe Henry as having judged the noblemen impartially, nor does it mention any attempts by the noblemen to regain his trust through submissiveness. Rather, Henry describes the noblemen as taking advantage of his patience and declares he will adopt a more commanding demeanor in the future. Choice C is incorrect. Although Henry concedes that he has perhaps been too calm and mild, Henry does not defend or vow to maintain his calm disposition. On the contrary, he explicitly states he will “from henceforth rather be myself, / Mighty and to be fear’d,” resolving to abandon the mild manner that has cost him the respect of the noblemen. Choice D is incorrect because Henry characterizes his manner as patient and mild—“smooth as oil, soft as young down”—not indifferent. Indifference implies a lack of concern, whereas Henry describes himself as being overly lenient. Additionally, although the final lines mention “the proud soul,” the focus is not on the noblemen’s excessive pride but rather on how Henry’s apparent lack of pride has caused him to lose the noblemen’s respect.
stem: The following text is adapted from William Shakespeare’s 1598 play Henry IV, Part 1. King Henry is addressing several noblemen who are rumored to have been disloyal to him.

KING HENRY: My blood hath been too cold and temperate, Unapt to stir at these indignities, And you have found me, for accordingly You tread upon my patience; but be sure I will from henceforth rather be myself, Mighty and to be fear’d, than my [disposition], Which hath been smooth as oil, soft as young down, And therefore lost that title of respect Which the proud soul ne’er pays but to the proud.
Which statement best describes how King Henry presents himself in the text?
